claim: USGS glossary: a phreatic eruption is a volcanic explosion that occurs when water contacts hot rocks or ash near a vent, causing steam explosions.
value: phreatic = steam explosion, water meets hot rock
source: USGS, Volcanoes of the United States, Glossary
note: Same text as reused in GEO-04. The current USGS Volcano Hazards glossary page returned an AWS challenge (HTTP 202, empty body) and was not bypassed.

claim: USGS: phreatic (steam-blast) eruptions are driven by expanding steam when cold ground or surface water meets hot rock or magma; they blast out only fragments of pre-existing solid rock from the conduit, and no new magma is erupted.
note: Quote limit: 'no new magma is erupted'. This is the line for the examiner's key (definition).

claim: USGS: phreatic activity is generally weak but can be quite violent, as in the 1965 eruption of Taal Volcano (Philippines) and the 1975-76 activity at La Soufriere, Guadeloupe.
value: weak to violent; Taal 1965, La Soufriere 1975-76
note: Deaths and damage at Taal 1965 and La Soufriere were not read, so no consequence figures are claimed for them.

claim: GeoNet (GNS Science): a phreatic eruption is driven by superheated steam and gas, often building up behind a rock-and-mineral seal until gas pressure exceeds its strength; the gas likely comes from a deeper magma source but the magma itself is not directly involved. Phreatic eruptions can also occur when hot magma meets cold groundwater, which GNS did not think was the case at Whakaari.
value: steam and gas behind a seal; magma not directly involved
source: GeoNet (GNS Science), Volcanic news item on Whakaari/White Island after the 9 Dec 2019 eruption (attributable to Brad Scott, GNS Science)
note: Two agencies word the cause differently (USGS: cold water meets hot rock or magma; GNS: gas pressure behind a seal, magma not directly involved). Both agree: steam-driven, no new magma erupted. Say 'steam-driven' and do not pick a side. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: as_of was "after 9 Dec 2019"; the saved page is dated 10 Dec 2019. Wording of the quoted passage verified. The page says magma-groundwater contact is not believed to be the case at Whakaari.

claim: Phreatomagmatic eruption (contrast): water and magma interact explosively and eject steam together with fragments of new magma. The USGS Volcano Hazards glossary entry could not be opened (bot challenge), so this is not confirmed at the publisher.
source: USGS Volcano Hazards Program glossary (seen only as a search-result snippet)
note: Not read at the publisher. The answer may still contrast with 'new magma erupted' using the USGS GIP line in row 02 (phreatic: no new magma).

claim: Whakaari/White Island (New Zealand) erupted at 2:11 pm NZST on 9 December 2019; it was a short event of 1-2 minutes that hit the Main Crater floor and put a steam and ash column to 12,000 ft (3-4 km) above the island. The alert level was raised from 1 to 2 on 18 Nov 2019.
source: GeoNet (GNS Science), Volcanic news item on Whakaari/White Island after the 9 Dec 2019 eruption (attributable to Brad Scott, GNS Science)
note: Update #10 (saved as sources/geonet_update10.txt) repeats '2:11pm on Monday 9 December'. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX (labelling): the GeoNet page explains what a phreatic eruption is but never states in words that the 9 Dec 2019 event was phreatic; read together the two sections imply it (our inference). Say "GeoNet describes Whakaari eruptions as steam-and-gas driven" or label the link ours. Also: the page says the Alert Level "was at Level 4" during the eruption (assigned afterwards); the Level 2 on 9 Dec is the level before the eruption, as the row states. Times, 1-2 min and 12,000 ft (3-4 km) verified.

claim: GeoNet: Whakaari is a wet volcano with a crater lake whose explosive eruptions occur with little to no warning and eject hot rocks (cannonball-like projectiles), ash clouds and surges (pyroclastic density currents). An eruption can occur at any Volcanic Alert Level, including Level 1 and 2.
source: GeoNet (GNS Science), Volcanic news item on Whakaari/White Island after the 9 Dec 2019 eruption (attributable to Brad Scott, GNS Science)
page_or_section: sections 'Eruption styles' and 'Is it unusual to go from Level 2 to an eruption?'
note: This is the agency statement on why such eruptions are hard to forecast. 'Even small eruptions can have devastating impacts' is on the same page.

claim: 22 people lost their lives in the Whakaari/White Island eruption (WorkSafe New Zealand, 30 Nov 2020, when it filed charges against 13 parties).
source: WorkSafe New Zealand, news release '13 parties charged ... Whakaari/White Island tragedy'
note: GeoNet pages do not give a death count; the Coroner's findings were not read; NZ History (nzhistory.govt.nz) returned a challenge page and was not used. NZ Police page read on 1 Dec 2019 said six dead then (early count, not used).

claim: GeoNet Update #10 (14 Dec 2019): no further eruptions since 9 Dec; the combined interpretation of all data was that magma is degassing at shallow depths and the situation remained highly volatile; some ash fell in the active vent area only.
note: Useful for 'consequences stay local': GeoNet news item says the island is about 50 km offshore, so mainland effects would be at most fine ash and gas smell.

claim: Mount Ontake (Japan) erupted at 11:52 JST on 27 September 2014.
source: Japan Meteorological Agency, Ontakesan (Mt. Ontake) Portal

claim: JMA booklet: at Ontake the ash plume rose about 7,000 m above the crater; ballistic projectiles were scattered about 1 km from the crater row; pyroclastic flows ran about 2.5 km southwest and 1.5 km northwest; ash eruptions continued to about 10 October. Japanese text: 58 dead, 5 missing, 69 injured; English text: 63 dead or missing (Fire and Disaster Management Agency, as of 6 Nov 2015).
value: plume 7 km; ballistics 1 km; 58 dead + 5 missing
source: Japan Meteorological Agency, Volcanoes: Volcano Monitoring and Disaster Mitigation (booklet)
second_source: Cabinet Office, Disaster Management in Japan 2024 white paper: 63 dead or missing
note: Figures differ by date: 58+5=63 here; the helium-anomaly paper seen only in a search snippet gave 57 dead and 6 missing and is not used.

claim: Japan's Cabinet Office calls the 2014 Ontake eruption a 'difficult-to-predict phreatic eruption', driven by rapid vaporisation and expansion of water from heating or depressurisation of underground water; it occurred suddenly among climbers (11:52 am on a fine weekend), 63 people dead or missing, more than 15,000 personnel in rescue operations until 16 October.
source: Cabinet Office, Government of Japan, Disaster Management in Japan 2024 (white paper)
note: This is the source that labels Ontake 'phreatic'; the JMA booklet passage does not use the word for Ontake.

claim: After Ontake, local governments kept entry restrictions even after the alert level was lowered to Level 1, and safety measures for climbers (evacuation facilities, a prefectural disaster management radio system) followed.
source: Cabinet Office, Government of Japan, Disaster Management in Japan 2024
